title: Legal representation changes the immediate housing-court path for poor tenants
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 29836; New York City Universal Access to Counsel rollout and address-level housing-court data
geography: New York City tenants and housing courts; address-level court data from 2016–2019

observations.period: New York City Universal Access to Counsel and tenant housing-court outcomes 2016–2019; paper issued 2022

denominator.unit: percent of federal poverty guideline income threshold for program eligibility

program.value: New York City's Universal Access program offered free housing-court legal representation to tenants with income at or below 200% of the federal poverty guideline

possessory_judgment.value: tenants who gained lawyers were less likely to be subject to possessory judgments

money_judgment.value: tenants who gained lawyers faced smaller monetary judgments

eviction_warrant.value: tenants who gained lawyers were less likely to have eviction warrants issued

completed_eviction.value: tenants who gained lawyers were less likely to be evicted

heterogeneity.value: lawyers had larger effects in poorer places and places with larger shares of noncitizens

observations.method: The authors use the rollout of New York City's Universal Access to Counsel program and detailed address-level housing-court data from 2016–2019 to estimate how gaining legal representation changes tenant outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not follow the same tenant through rent affordability, current arrears, payment plans, work, health, debt, credit, next housing, or long-term stability. It does not measure who could reach counsel before the hearing, lawyer capacity or quality, landlord recovery, or the full cost of the program.
observations.subgroup: New York City tenants eligible for or gaining representation under the Universal Access program, with larger effects in poorer places and places with more noncitizens; results may differ by landlord, neighborhood, housing supply, language, disability, and household structure.
observations.counterinterpretation: A better court outcome does not prove that rent became affordable or that the tenant's underlying income or health shock ended. A smaller money judgment may still be unaffordable, and avoiding a formal eviction may coexist with an informal move, a repayment burden, or later housing instability.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 29836

boundary: This record adds a court-access finding: New York City tenants who gained Universal Access legal representation had better immediate housing-court outcomes. It does not establish lasting housing stability, affordability, debt resolution, work or health recovery, or universal effects outside the program and city.
